title: The Human Is Not the Bottleneck. The Human Is the Missing Oracle
description:
We spent a year optimising the wrong bottleneck.

The harness discourse has been relentless - blueprints, schematics, thought leadership. Impressive engineering, most of it. But read the designs closely and you notice what they're all quietly aiming at: getting the developer out of the pipeline.

The logic seemed sound. Building dropped from days to minutes, and the human became the slow part. The bottleneck. So we designed the human out.

Then the telemetry arrived.

Faros AI instrumented 22,000 developers across 4,000+ teams. Moving from low to high AI adoption: task completion per developer up 34%, epics up 66%. Real gains. Also: bugs per developer up 54%, incidents per pull request up 243%, median review time up 5x, and 31% more PRs merging with no review at all.

Nobody decided to stop reviewing. Reviewers simply couldn't keep pace, and unread merges became normal. We knew this failure before AI. The 2,000-line PR lands in your inbox, and what follows is frustration, cognitive overload, and a silent rubber stamp. The difference is that it used to be the exception. Now it's the throughput model.

The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved to review and integration - and we'd already removed the person who was supposed to be standing there when it arrived.

Two things worth saying plainly.

First: the human was never the bottleneck. The human is the missing oracle.

We have fast, cheap oracles for correctness. Do the tests pass? Does it lint? Machine-verifiable in seconds. We have no oracle at all for maintainability, intent, or design - and no benchmark I'm aware of currently measures them. GitClear's analysis of 623 million code changes shows what fills that gap: duplication up 81%, refactoring down 70%, error-masking constructs up 47%. Code that looks right and is structurally wrong.

Designing the human out doesn't remove a cost. It removes the only sensor we have for the slowest and most expensive failure mode. "Humans first" isn't sentiment or ethics-washing. It's a claim about where verification capability actually resides right now.

Second: we're borrowing against comprehension and calling it velocity.

Anthropic ran a controlled trial in January. Two groups, same unfamiliar library. The AI-assisted group finished marginally faster and scored 50% on comprehension. The manual group scored 67%. Seventeen points, on code they had written minutes earlier (this is a vendor publishing a result against it's own commercial interest).

That debt doesn't show up in your DORA metrics. It shows up at 2am when nobody on the call can reason about the system they shipped.

The industry response is to build faster agents. So I built the opposite experiment. A harness that puts the human at the centre - not to slow things down, but to make judgment cheap, timely and measurable rather than optional. You can check out the harness here.

Plain bash. Deliberately crude. Built to learn, not to scale.

The rules:

  1. Agents don't move artefacts through the SDLC. They hit mechanical gates.
  2. Humans state intent, write the spec, define acceptance criteria, and read the diff.
  3. Route every check to the cheapest reliable verifier - mechanical gates for what's machine-checkable, calibrated LLM judges only after validation against human labels with explicit thresholds, humans for intent and design.
  4. Diff budget: 200 lines. (Which became 400, excluding tests). If it's more than 400 lines, the feature was scoped wrong. The gate fails and the work gets split.
  5. Only iterate on the harness with confirmed evidence and root cause.

Thirty minutes on an approved spec and a design sketch turns a six-hour adversarial review into a twenty-minute confirmation. The human isn't reviewing more. They're reviewing earlier, where a one-line correction prevents two thousand lines of rework.

237 minutes. 12 features. One engineer, no control group - an experiment, not evidence. I'm publishing the method so it can be argued with.

DORA's finding is that AI is an amplifier: it magnifies whatever your organisation already is. If your answer to a 243% rise in incidents per PR is to remove the last human who might have caught them, the amplifier is working exactly as designed.

What are you actually measuring?

KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

title: ChatGPT outage reminds users what life was like before AI
description:
There was a time not too long ago where last-minute essays were written overnight by adrenaline-filled students, work emails were carefully crafted using corporate lingo passed down by generations, and time-consuming busywork was a rite of passage for entry-level employees.

Now that AI has made its way into daily life, those days seem to be farther away than ever.

That is, unless ChatGPT is down.

In a recent OpenAI outage, ChatGPT Work—an agentic mode of the large language model (LLM) that lets you delegate tasks—was down for several hours, leaving users unable to initiate or continue tasks on the platform.

Many on social media initially reacted to the outage through comedy, jokingly saying that even a chatbot does not want to work on a Monday—the day the outage ocurred.

“The AI is like nah, need a day off,” one user joked, with another adding, “Calling in sick on a Monday is AGI.”

A user also responded to fears of AI-related job losses, joking: “I was worried AI would replace me but apparently we have the same work ethic.”

How sweet it was

But when OpenAI took to social media to update users on the outage and later report that the issue had been fixed, the response was not entirely one of excitement.

“And we’re back. Please resume outsourcing your thoughts immediately,” one user said in response to the update.

Another added: “Nice, I was dangerously close to doing the task myself.”

But beyond mockery, the brief AI-less moment for users brought back a sense of nostalgia about a world before ChatGPT, with many sharing their momentary bliss.

“Literally some of the happiest hours of my life, why’d you bring it back?” a user said on X in response to OpenAI’s update. Another added: “No need to fix. Shut it down and we’ll all be happy.”

The response is somewhat unsurprising with tensions between humans and artificial intelligence growing around the country. Despite 49% of American adults using AI chatbots in 2026, more than half of Americans have concerns over the use of AI in daily life.

While users were quick to return to using AI once service was reinstated, the outage did offer a momentary space for reflection on individuals’ reliance on the technology.

A user added: “The more powerful our tools become, the more uncomfortable it is when the tool itself becomes a single point of failure.”

title: Social media companies are using AI and face scans to spot more kids on their platforms
description:
Of the child safety measures agreed to in Meta’s landmark legal settlement, no category contains more detailed requirements than its commitments on age assurance—and for good reason. No matter how well the protections work, they are of little use if Meta can’t tell which users are kids.

Determining which accounts belong to children is also the linchpin of child safety measures that other companies, including Google, TikTok, and Roblox, are ramping up as public and regulatory sentiment turns against them in the U.S. and other countries.

The Meta settlement—with protections the company says could become industry standards—will give the social media giant a year to refine its approach. But the options are limited, and improving age verification technology presents steep challenges, including navigating privacy implications not just for children but for adults who could have to prove they are over 18.

The $18 billion settlement resolves claims from state attorneys general that it hurt children’s mental health by deliberately designing its Instagram and Facebook platforms in ways that hooked young people’s attention. The agreement announced last week with the Menlo Park, California, company involves 48 states plus the District of Columbia and U.S. territories.

Tech companies lean on AI for estimating ages

In the offline world, people use government-issued IDs to prove they are over 18 or 21, whether they want to get into a club or buy cigarettes. While this technically works online too, many people are not comfortable giving a Big Tech company like Meta or Google access to their driver’s license or passport.

Meta accepts IDs to check ages, and promises to delete them within 30 days. Beyond IDs, though, a growing number of tech companies are using artificial intelligence to try to determine users’ ages. This is not true age verification. While AI can estimate a person’s age, often accurately, it can’t verify a person’s birth date.

Last year, Google began using an age-assurance system for YouTube that relies on AI to differentiate between adults and minors based on their watch histories. Meta does the same.

AI age checks use clues to determine how old someone is. On Instagram, this includes “contextual clues” such as posts about birthday celebrations or school, and things like which posts people like, comment on, or linger on, who their friends are, as well as the times of day they log in. For instance, someone who is offline during school hours would likely be school-aged.

In a blog post last year, Meta said its AI also looks at photos people post for visual cues, including “height or bone structure, to estimate someone’s general age; it does not identify the specific person in the image.”

“By combining these visual insights with our analysis of text and interactions, we can significantly increase the number of underage accounts we identify and remove,” the company added.

Under the settlement, Meta agreed to strengthen its age-checking technology using its own tools, as well as third-party ones, with regular outside audits on how well it is working. The agreement also includes specific goals around false positive rates—that is, minors who are identified as over 18. And if a user is identified as under 13 and kicked off one of its platforms, Meta will check the ages of their friends, too.

Face scans count as age assurance on some sites

Identity verification companies like Yoti and Persona, which work with tech companies like Meta and Roblox, use video selfies people upload to estimate their ages.

The gaming site Roblox, which, unlike social media platforms, allows kids under 13 to sign up, requires players to take a video selfie to estimate their age. Roblox says the videos are deleted after the age check is processed. Users are not required to submit a face scan to use the platform, only if they want to chat with other users.

Some users have reported inaccuracies, and some experts have expressed caution about the reliability of facial age estimation tools, especially for women or certain racial or ethnic groups. But Matt Kaufman, chief safety officer at Roblox, said last year that for people between about 5 and 25, the system can accurately estimate their age within one or two years.

Some websites and social media companies such as Meta have argued that age verification should be done by app store owners, such as Apple and Google, and not individual platforms. This would mean that app stores would have to verify their users’ ages before they allow them to download apps. Unsurprisingly, Apple and Google disagree.

“Billed as ‘simple’ by its backers, including Meta, this proposal fails to cover desktop computers or other devices that are commonly shared within families. It also could be ineffective against pre-installed apps,” Google said in a blog post last year.

Privacy concerns remain an obstacle

Age checks are meant to keep kids out of online spaces that are not safe or appropriate for them, whether that’s social media or adult websites. But critics of online age verification see a worrisome trend toward a less secure, less private and less free internet, where people can be denied access not just to pornography but news, health information and the ability to speak openly and anonymously.

What’s considered harmful to minors can be subjective, and this is where experts believe laws requiring age verification can run afoul of the First Amendment. The question could lead to people being required to verify their ages to access anything, from Netflix to a neighborhood blog.

The digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation has been warning for years about “age-gating the internet.”

“(No) matter the method, every system demands users hand over sensitive and immutable personal information that links their offline identity to their online activity,” EFF writes in a blog post. “Once that valuable data is collected, it can easily be leaked, hacked, or misused.”

—Barbara Ortutay, AP technology writer

title: 401(k), IRA, or HSA? Here’s a hierarchy for retirement savings
description:
If you have a fixed sum of money to invest every month or every year, which investment account type gives you the biggest bang for your buck?

There are no one-size-fits-all answers, but this framework for retirement savings is a good starting point.

1: Invest enough in a 401(k)/other company retirement plan to earn matching contributions.

  1. Why: To take advantage of free money.
  2. Deprioritize if: Your 401(k) offers no matching contributions. In that case, proceed directly to No. 2.

Even a lackluster match—say, 25 cents per dollar—is hard to beat by investing outside the plan, and it comes on top of any investment earnings.

2: Invest in an IRA.

  1. Why: Low costs, flexibility, and the ability to contribute to a Roth.
  2. Deprioritize if: Your company retirement plan features all the bells and whistles, including ultralow costs and a Roth option.

Why choose an IRA over a 401(k)? IRAs often avoid administrative fees, and they offer an array of securities and a Roth option.

But if your 401(k) has no administrative expenses, ultralow-cost investments, and a Roth option, you can make a full 401(k) contribution before moving to an IRA.

2a: Invest in a Spousal IRA.

  1. Why: Amass retirement savings for a nonearning spouse.
  2. Deprioritize if: The 401(k) of the spouse with earnings is rock-solid; in that case, fully funding that 401(k) plan could reasonably come before funding IRAs for either spouse.

For married couples with a nonearning spouse, funding a spousal IRA should come next, if the earning spouse has enough to cover both.

3: Invest in your company retirement plan up to the limit.

  1. Why: The ability to enjoy tax-free contributions and tax-deferred compounding (traditional), or tax-free compounding and withdrawals (Roth).
  2. Deprioritize if: You have plenty of assets in accounts that will be taxed upon withdrawal, and you’re close to retirement. If that’s the case, you may want to prioritize saving in a taxable (nonretirement) account instead of maxing out the company retirement plan. Ditto if there’s a chance you’ll need the money before retirement.

Higher-income investors should generally exhaust all tax-sheltered retirement-savings options before investing in nonretirement accounts, even if their workplace plan isn’t best of breed. Traditional 401(k) contributions are pretax, compound tax-deferred, and reduce adjusted gross income, thereby increasing eligibility for credits and deductions. Roth 401(k)s offer tax-free compounding and withdrawals in retirement. Those benefits can make even a subpar 401(k) preferable to a taxable account.

4: Make health savings account contributions up to the limit.

  1. Why: Pretax contributions go in, funds can be invested and grow with tax benefits, and qualified withdrawals for healthcare outlays are also tax-free.
  2. Deprioritize if: You can’t contribute. You must be covered by a high-deductible health plan to contribute to an HSA.

HSAs can be treated as retirement saving vehicles if you invest the assets and let the money compound until retirement. Qualified withdrawals remain tax-free.

5: Make aftertax 401(k) contributions to the limit.

  1. Why: The ability to enhance a portfolio’s share of Roth assets, eventually—provided the 401(k) plan allows for the contribution of after-tax dollars.
  2. Deprioritize if: The 401(k) is especially poor or especially good, as outlined at the bottom of this article.

If you’ve maxed out regular 401(k) contributions of $24,500 ($32,500 if older than 50), you can contribute up to $72,000 total in 2026—provided your plan allows after-tax contributions. Then convert those to Roth inside the plan, if allowed, or once you retire, leave the company, or take in-service distributions.

This strategy is less attractive if you have a poor or costly 401(k).

6: Invest in a taxable account.

  1. Why: You’re aiming for tax diversification in retirement and already have a sizable share of your assets in tax-deferred and Roth accounts. Ditto if there’s a chance you’ll need to take out your money before retirement, or you expect to be in the 0% tax bracket for capital gains when you withdraw your money.
  2. Deprioritize if: You have more tax-advantaged account options available to you, and you have a long time horizon for your money.

With a taxable (nonretirement) account, you can invest in nearly anything, and there are no withdrawal requirements. You can access the money anytime, or let it build. And while you’ll invest after-tax dollars, you’ll owe capital gains taxes (lower than ordinary income taxes) when you sell.

This article was provided to The Associated Press by Morningstar. For more retirement content, go to https://www.morningstar.com/retirement.

Christine Benz is director of personal finance and retirement planning for Morningstar and co-host of The Long View podcast. Subscribe to her free newsletter, Improving Your Finances.

title: Waldkunstpfad in Darmstadt, Germany
description:
Hidden in the forest on the southern edge of Darmstadt, the Waldkunstpfad turns an ordinary woodland walk into something considerably more surreal. Along the trails, artworks emerge between the trees, lean against trunks, occupy clearings, or use the forest itself as part of the installation. Instead of entering a gallery, visitors simply follow the path and wait to see what the woods have decided to reveal.

The International Forest Art Trail has been running since 2002, with a new theme and a changing group of artists for each edition. Artists from around the world create site-specific works in and around the forest, often using natural or locally appropriate materials. Some pieces are bold and unmistakably artificial; others are so well integrated into their surroundings that they can initially look like something the forest produced on its own.

The result is part sculpture garden, part hiking trail, and part treasure hunt. A fallen branch might turn out to be an artwork. A peculiar wooden structure might suddenly make sense when viewed from the other side. Even familiar landmarks such as the Goethefelsen and Goetheteich become part of the experience.

The trail encourages slow exploration rather than a quick checklist of attractions. There is no grand museum entrance and no velvet rope separating art from nature. The forest is the gallery, the changing seasons are part of the exhibition, and discovering a work around the next bend is half the fun.

Many works remain in the forest beyond the official exhibition period, meaning the trail can continue to evolve between editions. The exact collection therefore depends on when it is visited—a useful excuse to come back and see what has appeared, disappeared, or been reclaimed by the woods.

The main route stretches through the Böllenfalltor forest toward Ludwigshöhe. Bring shoes suitable for woodland paths and keep an eye out: the most interesting artwork may not be the one that announces itself first.

title: Dispute With OpenAI Said to Be a 'Mess of Apple's Own Making'
description:
OpenAI yesterday denied Apple's allegations of trade secret theft, telling a federal court that Apple failed to show any confidential information was actually stolen by its former employees, according to Reuters.


In a new filing submitted to the U.S. District Court in San Jose, California, OpenAI argued that the dispute is "a mess of Apple's own making." The filing is a direct response to Apple's new forensic evidence submitted against former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan, whom Apple accuses of stealing trade secrets related to hardware design, manufacturing, and supply chain operations after filing the lawsuit in July.

OpenAI says the lawsuit is an attempt to slow a rival and deter more employee departures. In court filings, it notes that it has hired about 400 former Apple employees for its hardware projects. The company argues that California law allows workers to move freely between competitors, while shifting attention to Apple's internal practices instead of addressing the forensic evidence allegation by allegation.

OpenAI alleges that Apple encourages staff to use personal iCloud accounts for work, potentially blurring the boundary between personal and company data after an employee leaves. It also says Apple's practice of immediately escorting departing employees off site leaves too little time to return devices or internal files, portraying the allegations as the result of a flawed offboarding process rather than intentional theft.

The filing says Liu retained access to Apple documents only to help former colleagues find files or answer questions, and that Apple employees repeatedly contacted him for support. Tan said he returned his Apple prototypes before leaving and kept only non-confidential materials, including a standard departure checklist.

OpenAI characterized the dispute as employees choosing to leave a company it says has been slow to adopt AI for a faster-moving competitor. It argued that Apple should not use its own internal failures to portray those departures as unlawful. Judge Edward J. Davila is scheduled to hear arguments on October 1.
Tags: Apple Lawsuits, OpenAI

This article, "Dispute With OpenAI Said to Be a 'Mess of Apple's Own Making'" first appeared on MacRumors.com

title: Adam’s Gulch  in Ketchum, Idaho
description:
Mountain bikers and hikers pour into Adam’s Gulch for its 33 miles of interconnected trails, but the gulch has a quieter claim to attention: more than a century ago, it was home to an early ranger station in what became the Ketchum Ranger District.

After the Sawtooth National Forest was established in 1905, its territory was divided into ranger districts, with the first ranger’s station at Adam’s Gulch built in 1909. The district’s administrative center later moved elsewhere, leaving the gulch to become better known for recreation than bureaucracy.

Today, Adam’s Gulch Trailhead is the most popular trailhead in the Ketchum Ranger District. The network begins just outside Ketchum and offers routes ranging from a quick outing on Sunnyside Trail to mountain biking on Forbidden Fruit and longer adventures toward Fox Peak.

The setting helps explain the appeal. Trails thread through the foothills and connect into a much larger network around the Wood River Valley. Wildlife is very much part of that landscape. Idaho Fish and Game has documented both black bears and moose in the Adams Gulch area and has reminded visitors to give wild animals plenty of space.

title: ‘They take the water, the springs dry up’: fear as Guatemalan goldmine plan is revived
description:

Ramírez’s home lies less than a mile from Era Dorada – a goldmining project acquired by the Canadian multinational Aura Minerals in January 2025. After years of inactivity, the project was reactivated this year when the Guatemalan government granted Aura a construction licence.

title: Which local LLM should you run?
description:
whichllm is a useful Python CLI utility that autodetects your GPU/CPU/RAM and pulls benchmarks from Hugging Face to rank the local LLMs you can run on your system, based on a mix of benchmarks and projected token speeds on your machine.

I have a modest but respectable 16 GB of NVIDIA VRAM at my disposal, so unsurprisingly the top models it suggests for my hardware are in the Qwen 3 and Phi 4 families, as well as the always excellent gpt-oss-20b from OpenAI. These suggestions basically match my own experiments.

The top suggestion is Qwen3.6-27B, but the tool is basing it on stale benchmarks from May 2026 (I got a rate limiting error when it tried to pull the live benchmarks—I guess a lot of people are clamoring to test local LLMs).

If the tool was using live benchmarks, I believe it would almost certainly put Qwen3.8-27B at the very top, the model released a few weeks ago to rave reviews.

I was also curious which models it would recommend if I was running on CPU only. Surprisingly, the top suggestion was gpt-oss-20b, with a warning that all of the top contenders would run very slowly and that token speed estimates were uncertain.

title: Luke Mitchell on Design Process
description:
Tell us a little bit about yourself

I have been a designer of one sort or another since 2011. I started out as a Graphic Designer who also built websites, but as I got more and more interested in web apps and websites I started moving towards digital design then product design.

I am currently Lead Product Designer at Definely. I am happy working on design at any step of the process, whether that be strategy, research, prototyping, testing, design systems, and everything in between.

I also love to code when I get the chance, I am a big fan of HTML and CSS, but I will give most languages a try.

What are the first questions you ask at the beginning of every project?

  • What research do we already have?
  • Has any design work already been done?
  • What resources do we have to share?
  • Where did this idea come from? (support ticket, stakeholders etc.)
  • How urgent is it? (should I drop other things I’m working on to start on this?)
  • Who is the team that will be working on it?

How do you approach pricing with clients? How did you arrive at this?

I’ve never been freelance or been directly involved in too many pricing conversations, but I often need to estimate how long things will take. I usually start with a broad estimate followed by frequent updates, I like to over estimate and then take anything ahead of schedule as a win.

What are the first things you do when you start a new project?

I don’t usually do anything concrete, and it depends on the project. But I will usually start by ask a bunch of questions, and then outline the next steps I will take. I will try and learn as much as I can about the problem, from there I see where the wind takes me and go from there.

What does your moodboarding process look like? Where do you source inspiration?

I don’t moodboard as often I as used to, but when I do my sources vary. I tend to avoid just moodboarding bits of UI/UX, as that has too much of a bias for solutions. Instead I try to find an eclectic mix of sources, my favourites include architecture, interior design, photography, typography, and physical product design.

I read a lot articles from blogs and sites I like via RSS, and I save visuals I find inspiring on Savee.

What’s your favourite part of the design process? Why?

Prototyping. It’s great to move fast and get something out of your head, then test it with people quickly. I would love to have a number on the amount of hours I’ve saved on circular discussions about features by just building a little thing and showing it to people, it clarifies and validates faster than any amount of meetings could.

Are there any parts of your process that go against received wisdom? Or common steps that you skip? Why?

There have been times where I followed the ‘double diamond’ process religiously, but more often than not I tend to let the process reveal itself as move along. It really depends on the feature or product, but I find you can often skip a super in-depth discovery process for something far less formal and time consuming.

Similarly I often find that having a long iterative process of design drafts doesn’t really lead anywhere productive, sometimes shifting focus too much into detail too early in a project. I prefer to research to confirm assumptions, and then iterate on a shipped feature instead of iterating before launching anything at all.

Less double diamond and more squiggly line.

Is there anything else you suspect is unique or unusual about your practice?

I create lots of diagrams, which I don’t see very often from designers, I see it more from engineers and developers: Information architecture, user flows, workflows, swimlanes, all sorts. I think that it helps to get information structured and out of my head without a UI early. It really helps to focus on all those little words and connections, when you aren’t biased by colours, layout typography etc.

If you collaborate with others (copywriters, illustrators, developers, etc): when do you bring them in? How do you handle project management?

Early and often, if they’re curious to get involved. It can be very helpful to have a small team involved throughout the whole process. There have been plenty of times where a developer has asked a key question during a research interview, or a product manager has noticed an early inefficiency in my thinking, that would not have been caught until we were much further along otherwise.

What’s been the most impactful change you’ve made to your process? Where did you hear about it?

Asking “stupid” questions. I have learnt so much by asking questions that should have an obvious answer, and avoided massive assumptions early on. For example say somebody I’ve never worked with before mentions a “customer”, I will ask “What does ‘customer’ mean?”. The answer is often far more nuanced and unexpected than you might think.

Unfortunately I can’t remember where or when I first started doing this.

What parts of the process are non-negotiables for you?

Honestly, I’m happy to skip any part if there is a good reason to do so. I often have strong opinions on validating assumptions, and prototyping, but even those can be ditched in some projects.

How do you organise design files?

I’m not very good at this. I will occasionally have a blitz and a tidy up when things get overwhelming inside Figma. But if I’m handing anything over I’ll usually create a page with the name of a Linear ticket, and send links to that out.

What does design hand-off look like for you?

It depends on what I’m designing, if it’s a little change all that needed is a quick comment or Slack message. But as things get more complex I will document more heavily and write specs as needed, I’m not a pixel-perfect kind of guy.

I will also have short calls with the team and present the design and answer questions as they come up, and then document that instead if the feature is particularly big. I will often get involved directly with front-end code also if it saves a developer putting up with me listing 50 ‘snags’ that I’d like fixed.

Looking back over the last 12 months, how do people find out about you?

I’m not much of a self-promoter, I get a fair bit of traffic to my website, especially the bookmarks page, but it’s not something I actively push or post about anywhere else. I’m lucky to only have had to look for work once or twice in the last 10 years, both times I applied for those jobs. If I were ever to go freelance I would have to be much more proactive.

What elements of the process create speed bumps or challenges? How do you get out of these ruts?

I find projects often get stuck in a discussion loop, or lose momentum when the task seems a bit too big. I try to break that loop by doing or building something demonstrable that everyone can see, critique, and plan against. It’s easier to say if something works or doesn’t, or if it’s too ambitious, if you can see and use it.

How do you make decisions?

There are lots of factors to take into account for decision-making: time, urgency, impact etc. If it’s a short-term, low-impact, urgent decision I usually use experience and intuition to get those out of the way quickly. I know that the decision I make there is probably reversible and I can iterate on it later.

The trickier ones are the decisions where I care much more about the outcome, usually because it has long-term impact that would be hard to reverse quickly. In those cases I have to make sure I am prepared to answer any questions that might counter my opinion, I also like to be prepared with resources to back my decision up. If I can’t justify my decision with anything more than “because I think it’s right”, then I haven’t done my job.

That being said I am surrounded by smart people who I listen to when making decisions, and while I will push back I will concede or compromise when others have similarly well prepared arguments to mine.

Favourite tool, resource or course?

Physical: A nice pen and a nice notebook.

Digital: Things by Cultured Code.

Where can people find out more about you, keep up to date, or work with you?

Checkout my website, there are some other links on there: interroban.gg

title: AI is making us sound the same—and killing our personal expression
description:
More than a third of all internet web pages published since ChatGPT’s November 2022 launch were authored by AI, according to the Pew Research Center. And the writing is becoming simpler than ever.

That flood of AI-generated language may also be changing the way humans write. A new paper in Nature Human Behavior finds that LLMs can push people’s writing toward a narrower set of linguistic norms, reducing stylistic diversity and obscuring some of the identity signals embedded in our words.

Three years ago, lead researcher Zhivar Sourati read The Secret Life of Pronouns: What Our Words Say About Us, James Pennebaker’s book that explored how people’s personal values, backgrounds, and beliefs can lead them to communicate the same ideas using different words. At the same time, LLMs were becoming more popular, and Sourati began to wonder whether the tech might reduce that linguistic diversity.

“We were kind of asking, what would actually happen when everyone’s text is going through the same models?” Sourati says. “If you have this layer on top of everyone’s text, would you change any of these artifacts that we know about people’s texts? Would it affect it in any significant way? What are the implications?”

So, he set to work to find out. First, Sourati conducted a time-series analysis using approximately 80,000 academic papers, 400,000 news articles, and 300,000 Reddit stories written before and after ChatGPT’s introduction. He found that after the adoption of AI writing tools, variation in writing complexity increasingly converged toward common stylistic norms. The trend was consistent across all three datasets.

Next, Sourati and his team conducted a more traditional experiment. They had GPT-3.5, Gemini, and Meta’s Llama 3 rewrite human-authored texts using a variety of prompts. While the models largely preserved the texts’ meaning, they reduced variation in writing complexity 21% to 50%.

But Sourati wanted to get more specific about the societal implications: How are LLMs eroding the signals of individual identity in our writing?

His team turned to texts written by people whose personal traits had been identified through psychological questionnaires. As in the earlier experiment, they fed the texts through an LLM. Statistical models were then used to predict traits—including demographics, personality, empathy, and moral values—based on linguistic features. After the texts were polished with AI, predictive accuracy declined by an average of 6%.

In the study’s third stage, Sourati explored exactly what was being erased. The results weren’t uniform. LLMs altered different linguistic signals in different ways depending on the personal trait being analyzed.

Sourati believes relying on LLMs to do all of your writing could have dangerous implications. The kind of problem-solving necessary in today’s world, he argues, depends on cognitive diversity, not just linguistic diversity.

“That’s the scary part,” Sourati tells Fast Company. “Because if everyone is using LLMs, then they have the ability to rewrite what’s the socially correct way of saying something, or what’s a credible way of having a perspective.”

Sourati hopes there’s a future in which diversity becomes a design principle in the development of large language models. He believes the people most vulnerable to their homogenizing effects are those still developing their cognitive abilities, particularly students.

He says people need to learn to think for themselves first. Then they can use LLMs more creatively.

“If you already know how to reason through something, then maybe you can use these models to kind of just have their good sides,” Sourati says, “without having all the destructive effects that they have on collective problem-solving abilities.”

title: I was co-CEO of a $100 million company. Here’s how my sense of urgency nearly killed it
description:
Over the course of a long career, I’ve made my share of mistakes, but the dumbest and most damaging ones have always been driven by urgency. Whenever I convinced myself that an opportunity was so great I had to “strike while the iron is hot,” boneheaded decisions inevitably followed, usually ending in some crushing failure.

Of course, nobody ever tells you that because “creating a sense of urgency” is supposed to be a good thing. It leads to action, and action feels good. Deliberation, on the other hand, can feel frustrating and, let’s face it, boring. If you can create urgency, you can make things happen. The problem is that the things you make happen are often the wrong ones.

That was certainly true of the worst mistake I ever took part in. In 2007, our company in Kyiv hatched a plan to dominate Ukrainian-language media. At the time, there were no significant competitors, despite credible research suggesting substantial unmet demand. What looked like a once-in-a-generation opportunity turned into a catastrophe. It nearly killed the company.


The emergence of an idea

Our company, KP Media, was founded in 1995 by Jed Sunden, a 25-year-old native of Brooklyn. It started with the Kyiv Post, which he financed with $8,000 on his credit card. Mirroring the Ukrainian economy at the time, the company grew in fits for the first five or six years, but by the time I joined in 2004 it had become a significant enterprise with roughly 200 employees.  

By that time, change was in the air and our Russian-language newsweekly, Korrespondent, became very much a symbol of that change. The Orange Revolution brought not only record foreign investment to Ukraine, but also newfound interest in a free press. Ukrainian citizens—as well as advertisers—demanded accurate, objective news sources.

We dominated that market in print and online. Our business began to grow by leaps and bounds. As Ukraine became a hot market, there was increasing interest in us from investors; in 2007, we went public at a valuation of roughly $50 million, which was an enormous amount of money in Ukraine at the time. Before you knew it, our stock price doubled and we became a $100 million company.

That’s what led us to what we thought was a truly revolutionary idea. 

Ukraine had long been a bilingual country. During the Soviet era, Russian had been the official language, even though at home and with friends, most people spoke Ukrainian. But after Ukraine became an independent country in 1991, Ukrainian became the official language. On TV, programming was required to be in the Ukrainian language, but Russian-language media still dominated in print and online.

To us, the opportunity seemed obvious. If we moved early into Ukrainian-language media, just as we had in online news, we could dominate the market.

Devising a strategy

Not wanting to rely just on a hunch, we began to research the market. Historically, the most lucrative areas were in the industrial eastern provinces that were closer to Russia culturally and linguistically. But the western, more European-oriented cities, where the Ukrainian language was more deeply ingrained, were beginning to prosper. We also saw decent traffic on the Ukrainian versions of our websites. 

As we delved more deeply into the research, we found that a significant portion of the population actually preferred Ukrainian-language media. It seemed that we had identified an attractive market with pent-up demand. Because we were using publicly available research, we also expected that others would soon be rushing in to take advantage of the opportunity. There were plenty of signs that we were on to something.

So we decided to move forward aggressively. We hired an editorial director from Poland to oversee development of two women’s magazines—a monthly and a weekly. Similar in format and theme to Good Housekeeping, these were designed to appeal to women working to balance marriage, family, and work life. We also began working on a Ukrainian newsweekly to complement our hit product, Korrespondent. 

That would mean three major product launches within a year, in addition to the daily newspaper we had already launched recently. If successful, we would essentially double the size of our print media business. We knew that would stretch our resources to the limit, or even past that. Still, it seemed like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and we didn’t want to miss it. 

Taking the plunge

We started with the monthly women’s magazine. We hired a great team, designed the format, and developed the brand. Our sales operation pushed aggressively to secure advance commitments from advertisers and distributors. Unfortunately, both copy sales and ad sales were disappointing. Many were skeptical about the market for Ukrainian-language print media. 

Still, we had seen slow launches turn into successful products before, so we weren’t overly worried. After all, we’d done our homework, were confident in our track record of bringing original new products to market, and, as a major media company, had the marketing muscle to maintain massive promotional activity indefinitely. 

So we pressed on with the other two launches, still nervous that someone else would see the genius of our plan and copy it. Over the next six months we built out two additional editorial teams, one for the women’s weekly magazine and one for the newsweekly magazine. We built strong marketing programs for each and brought them to market. 

By summer 2008, our confidence began to wane. All three product launches had been flops. We’d also begun to hear strange murmurs about problems with the housing market in the U.S. It all seemed fairly remote to us in Ukraine, but I had some knowledgeable contacts who were beginning to speak in hushed tones about the health of the financial markets. 

We expected if there were a major global recession that Ukraine would take a hit, but its economy had been expanding by about 8% per year. We were fairly certain that even if there were a slowdown, growth would continue.

We were wrong. 

Hard lessons

Clearly, investing in Ukrainian-language magazines in 2007 was a bad decision. Launching three titles within 12 months in an unproven market was catastrophic. It very nearly killed our company. When the global financial crisis hit in 2008, the bottom fell out of the Ukrainian economy. GDP contracted a whopping 15%. The ad market dropped 85%. 

It felt apocalyptic. Every day on the way to work, I would look at the exchange kiosks showing the Ukrainian currency crashing in value. When I arrived at the office, there would be a series of excruciating decisions to make. We closed all the new brands we launched since our initial public offering. At one point, I had to fire 150 people in a day, not because they had failed us, but because we, blinded by hubris and stupidity, had failed them.

The real tragedy was that if we had been more methodical, the cash from our IPO would likely have sustained us through the crisis. In fact, having cash when very few others did would have put us in a great position. But we were sure we were on to the next big thing. We felt a profound sense of urgency to beat everyone else to the punch and moved forward at breakneck speed. 

I wish I could say I learned my lesson then, but I didn’t. The same pattern persisted. I would get excited by an idea, convince myself I was on to something important, and rush to move forward. What I learned over time is that we are incredibly poor judges of our own ideas and that we need to take a Bayesian approach, moving forward steadily, iterating and testing as we go.

The truth is that every idea is wrong. Some are off by a little, and some are off by a lot, but they are all, to some degree, wrong. The key isn’t to come up with the “right” ideas, but to make them less wrong over time.

title: Your leaders are not okay
description:
A regular pattern that I have observed with my senior-level executive coaching clients is that they seem to be doing great but in reality are struggling. On the surface, they look successful: excellent results, composure under pressure, and abundant confidence in all the right settings. They wear the mask of executive presence. But underneath, they’re exhausted, and no one close to them notices or feels able to speak up.

This was brought home to me in a comment on one of my recent LinkedIn posts about the importance of human connection at work: “The person who just won Leader of the Year can be silently falling apart, and nobody notices because the performance is so good it looks like thriving. By the time it shows up on a dashboard, it’s not just expensive. It’s already downstream. Their team is carrying it. The culture is shaped by it. And nobody can name why.”

Loneliness and disconnection at work are endemic at all levels. At senior levels, these are among the most expensive, least visible problems in organizations today.

Being alone is about structure. Being lonely is about relationships

The reality of the organizational structure chart is as you move through your career, you have fewer peers, increased scrutiny, and decisions you can’t share with the broader organization. It comes with the territory. The higher you go, the fewer people can see or understand your daily reality. 

Loneliness at the top is something else entirely. It’s what happens when the structural reality of being the only person in the seat is amplified by having no one around you who sees past your title to the person underneath. There’s no one who thinks to ask how you really are, no one you can share your up and down moments with, and fewer people who listen with empathy or provide honest feedback. You’re seen as a leader first and a human second.

Being alone can be managed. But you can’t solve loneliness by changing the org chart or joining another board. Only better workplace relationships can help close the connection gap. 

Data every organization should pay attention to

The 2025 Fearless Report, based on Amy Edmondson’s research with more than 5,500 professionals in 33 countries, found that loneliness at work reduces psychological safety by half. Those who always felt lonely scored 42 on the psychological safety index, while those who never felt lonely scored 80, a 38-point difference.

When loneliness takes hold, people stop speaking up and challenging ideas. They stop having honest disagreements that raise the bar. The warning signs that something is wrong don’t disappear; people just stop voicing them. By the time the impact shows up in the numbers, the damage has been building for months.

One in 25 professionals responding to the 2025 Fearless Report shared that they always feel lonely at work. Research I conducted confirms this: In a dataset from more than 1,500 leaders, one in five reported having no meaningful workplace relationships at all. This is a leadership crisis hiding in plain sight. 

When the mask becomes the trap 

At a gathering of executive coaches, Alan Mulally, former CEO of Ford and Boeing, told a story that stuck with me. He realized that as CEO, “his face was no longer his own.” If he looked worried, people would talk: “Did you see the CEO’s face in that meeting?” Soon, it would turn into “something’s wrong.” A simple moment of concentration could become an organizational crisis by the time it reached the second floor.

As a result, leaders learn to manage their emotions, to mask what they’re really thinking and feeling. To some extent, that’s responsible leadership. As my colleague, Ruby Vesely, will often share with the leaders and teams she coaches, “Your energy affects everyone in the room and shapes what happens there. You bring the weather; are you bringing sunshine or storm clouds?” 

Being mindful of the energy you bring isn’t just for show. It’s part of your job.

But the mask that protects the organization can also trap the person wearing it. “I’m fine,” or “It’s fine,” work when things genuinely are fine. But what happens when things aren’t going according to plan? What happens when the leader behind the mask is struggling, and the mask has become so convincing that nobody thinks to look behind it? Or the leader dare not take the mask off?

I will never forget my first meeting with a CEO who was considering working with me as his coach. Within minutes he started to cry. He kept apologizing. I simply gave him the space to move through the moment. 

He was in the early days of a family bereavement, but hadn’t felt able to share that with anyone on his team. He was the poster child for “keep calm and carry on.” His mask was firmly in place, and had been for weeks, until I sensed he was carrying something heavy and asked a question that gave him permission to take it off. 

Our conversation didn’t remove his grief, but it did give him something he hadn’t had since the loss, someone who saw him as a human being first and a CEO second. 

His experience isn’t unusual. The underlying emotions behind the mask don’t fade just because they’re hidden. They ferment. Grief impacts how you show up everyday, frustration curdles into resentment, and doubt can harden into paralysis. The pressure continues to build, amplified by loneliness and the misbelief that it’s just you, that everyone else is handling this, that you’re the one who’s broken.

You’re not broken. You’re isolated, and there is a difference.

Contrary to popular belief, senior leaders are human too! They experience the same trials and tribulations as the rest of us: health scares, family crises, financial stress, self-doubt, grief. The difference is that the higher you go, the less permission you have to do any of those things publicly. “Everything’s fine” becomes the default response. And because the results are still coming in, you’re hitting your targets, nobody thinks to ask how you’re doing, only to celebrate what you’re doing. 

Until, that is, everything’s not fine, you’re not fine. And by then, the damage is already further downstream in the organization. Your team has sensed things are different, even if they can’t name what. They’ve been absorbing the stress, compensating for decisions that didn’t get made clearly, navigating conversations that never happened. The team’s culture has been shaped by a leader running on empty, and nobody can name why, because from the outside it still looked like it was thriving.

What you can do about it

This isn’t a wellness problem. And it won’t be solved by telling leaders—or yourself—to be more resilient. Resilience assumes the individual is the problem. Loneliness at the top isn’t a personal deficiency to be toughened through. It’s a relationship gap. And it requires deliberate action, intention, and attention to your relationships.

1. Start by asking yourself: Who in your professional life would tell you you’re not okay, even if you said you were? In my book, Cultivate: The Power of Winning Relationships, I call this person an Ally, a truth-speaker who supports your success no matter what. At the most senior levels, these relationships can be more challenging to maintain. Most people may choose to tell you what you want to hear because honesty can be risky. But that risk goes both ways. It can be career limiting for them if they speak up, and a career risk for you if they don’t. It’s your responsibility to nurture those relationships and the culture that allows for candor. If you can’t name your Ally, someone you can be honest with and who can be honest with you, you’re not just alone at the top, you risk being lonely.

2. Find your truth-speaker. It can be a peer from another company, a former colleague, a coach, or a mentor. What matters isn’t their rank or expertise, but their willingness to be honest with you, especially when it’s hard. If you don’t have this relationship, building it is the best investment you can make in your leadership. 

3. Stop pretending everything is “fine.” Next time someone asks how you’re doing, and you’re not okay, try giving a slightly more honest answer. You don’t have to share everything you’re thinking and feeling, but even saying, “I’m carrying a lot right now” or, “This quarter has been harder than it looks,” can be enough to create a moment of connection. When you’re honest, you encourage others to do the same.

The loneliest leaders are hiding in plain sight

They’re in your leadership meetings. They’re on stage at your company events. They’re delivering results that make everyone assume they’re fine. And they may be wondering if anyone would notice if they weren’t.

The question isn’t whether they are performing; of course they are. This is how they got to the top. The question is whether they feel connected to even one person beyond their job title, and whether anyone around them has the relationship, the courage, and care to ask what that performance is costing them.

If you’re a senior leader and this sounds at all familiar, you don’t need another program or leadership book. You need one person who can see past your results. And if you’re the colleague, board member, or friend to a senior leader, be the person who asks how they’re really doing, and stays for the real answer.

The loneliest leaders won’t tell you they’re lonely. That’s the whole point. Somebody has to go first.

title: Harness Engineering Simplified
description:
Two terms are rapidly entering the software vocabulary and they describe two very different answers to the same question: if AI agents write our code, what do we build around them to ensure quality, consistency and reliability?

Harness Engineering

A harness is defined as a piece of equipment with straps and belts, used to control or hold in place a person, animal or object. Some examples are a safety harness if you are doing bungee. Or a baby's harness. Historically, a harness was very much associated with draft animals such as horses, oxen, mules and cattle. An ox pulling a plow is typically yoked with a harness. The intent was to harness something effectively. That is: to direct, control, and use its power effectively for a purpose.

A harness in AI, is everything you put around an AI agent to shape how it works and to check what it produces. The discipline is broken into 3 parts. Guides steer the work forward. These are (a) rules and context files, (b) specs and prompts (c) skills and examples and (d) tools the agent may leverage. The second part is Boundaries - constraints for effective execution. These include sandboxes for isolation, permissions and token budgets. This ensures that the agent is constrained to run safely, but also run in a loop within some predefined resource limitations. The final part is Sensors. These verify the result. This is done with compilers, linters, tests, security scans and increasingly AI reviewers.

Harness engineering is the craft of combining these deliberately. Early evidence suggests it reduces token consumption, makes output markedly more consistent, and that specific named instructions dramatically outperform general guidance. But there's a catch: the most effective harnesses appear to be those co-developed with their backing models. Harness and model trained and tested together. That's part of why Claude Code punches above its weight, and it raises an uncomfortable question for us around our own.

Software Factory

A factory is a set of buildings where large amounts of goods are made using machines. A software factory is the same idea, where a set of systems are integrated to build, verify and release software repeatedly and at scale, with AI agents as machinery.

The software factory is the harness taken to its logical extreme: remove the humans. A backlog of work items feeds an orchestrator. An orchestrator dispatches an agent swarm to do the various parts of the work. Automated checks gate the output - AI reviews the AI's work and merges it. Deployment is continuous. And telemetry or feedback generates the next tickets. The loop runs and closes without a person standing anywhere on the line of production. Its promise is throughput. Code generation around the clock at near-zero marginal human cost.

Harness engineering will mature into a discipline - from individual craft to team practice and then platform capability, with shared harness components governed centrally and judgement federated back to the teams on the ground. Two problems will define these steps forward, sensor integrity. That is, how accurate, useful and reliable are the sensors we build. The second is, calibration - AI judges are proliferating faster than anyone is measuring them, and the harnesses that endure will be the ones that score their automated reviewers (AI) against human decisions over time and improve through it.

Software factories will find their niche and their ceiling. Factories are genuinely viable when correctness is cheap to verify, and errors are cheap to reverse - transactional back-ends, legacy rewrites governed by strong conformance test suites and internal tooling. The ceiling is structural. Today's models are trained against fast signals - does it compile, do tests pass, and are lint checks clean. However, what they do not cater for is design, maintainability, fidelity to intent and these things will surface over the months for which no automation checks. A factory has no station for slow signals, so it doesn't fail loudly. It instead accrues debt silently behind green checkmarks.

Conclusion The two concepts are not rivals so much as two settings of one dial: how much do we let an agent decide, and how we stay confident in what it does? The answer depends on the situation. If you can check the result cheaply and trust the check, the agent can be given more freedom. If checking is hard or mistakes are expensive, keep the leash short. We need to place human judgement where it matters most - saying what correct means at the start, and making the final call at the end. But we must also regularly test whether the automated judges in between can still be trusted.

title: The Balearic Social Housing Model Receives the 2026 OBEL Award
description: Amid growing economic, political, and climatic instability, the 2026 OBEL Award highlights the need for architectural approaches that rethink both existing and emerging infrastructures. The title for this edition is "Systems' Hack," where "systems" are understood as interrelated mechanisms governed by shared rules and "hacking" is framed as a strategic intervention that seeks to alter how these mechanisms operate. Within this framework, the OBEL Foundation has announced the Balearic Social Housing Model as the winner of this year's award, while also announcing a new cycle in 2027 under the same topic. The Balearic Social Housing Model is recognized for "transforming the role of social housing administration in the Balearic Islands between 2019 and 2023," proposing new approaches in response to an acute housing shortage and a critically limited public rental housing stock in Spain.

title: Apple Says Former Engineer Used Stolen Trade Secrets at OpenAI, Taught AI Agent to Run Them
description:
Apple today submitted new evidence in its lawsuit against OpenAI, with the hope that the new information will persuade the judge to grant an expedited discovery process.


Apple filed a theft of trade secrets lawsuit against OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan in July, accusing them of using multiple methods to steal data from Apple. Liu kept an Apple-issued MacBook after he left for OpenAI, and Apple got it back after the lawsuit was filed. Apple now says forensic analysis of the laptop has uncovered more evidence of Liu's use of Apple information and his attempts to hide what he'd done.

From the lawsuit:

  • Mr. Liu not only downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic but also used it in his work at OpenAI;

  • Far from his unauthorized access to Apple's third-party cloud storage being unknown to him, Mr. Liu and others at OpenAI were well-aware of that access;

  • Mr. Liu, upon learning of Apple's internal investigation of him, sent instructions for destroying evidence to an OpenAI colleague who confirmed she would comply; and

  • Mr. Liu used a tool in his work at OpenAI that has the same name as an internal Apple engineering application used for Apple development work.


Liu downloaded the circuit schematic from Apple in March, two months after he left the company. Liu used the schematic to run a simulation using electrical engineering tool LTspice, and then messaged people telling them he ran the simulation for power conversion development work. Liu described how he trained an AI agent to run LTspice.

According to the filing, he said he was "[f]eeling AI all day long," and that "[i]n the past hour," his AI "agent learned how to run LTspice, look at result, tune compensation parameter." "I try to make a behavior buck," he wrote. "With voltage outer and current inner. Everything ideal. It still took me a day.. now it's two hour. Including learning fresh."

"Oh man! Why do they even need you then?" the person Liu was talking to reportedly replied.

Liu used the Apple schematic on a Mac mini that later synced to the MacBook he took from Apple, which is why Apple knows about it. Apple now wants to investigate the ‌Mac mini‌ and other devices Liu still has in his possession.

Apple says the "shocking evidence" is proof that its trade secrets are in active use and evidence is being destroyed, which is why expedited discovery is needed.

Apple initially asked for expedited discovery earlier this month, also requesting an injunction preventing OpenAI from using its trade secrets. OpenAI responded by asking the court to dismiss the lawsuit, claiming the accusations were "meritless." OpenAI also published a public statement calling the lawsuit "careless, aggressive and oddly personal" and stating that it does not "have, nor want, any of their trade secrets" because it is "much more interested in building innovative products and technologies that push the frontier."

Judge Edward J. Davila is set to hear arguments in the case on October 1.
Tag: OpenAI

title: Recalled guacamole hits FDA’s highest risk level. Here’s what could happen if you eat it
description:
If you have guacamole from Whole Foods in your refrigerator, you might want to check its best-by date. The Food and Drug Administration has classified a recent recall of mild guacamole and salsa dips sold at Whole Foods Market as Class I, the most serious type of recall, over potential salmonella contamination.

According to recall guidance from the FDA, a recall of this nature means there is “reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to” the recalled item “will cause serious adverse health consequences or death.”

The recall, initiated on August 7, includes 10 different varieties of guacamole and salsa dip and impacts 12,995 units of the refrigerated product. The best-before or best-by dates range from August 7, 2026, to August 16, 2026. The full list of products in various sizes and their PLU codes can be found here.

No illnesses have been reported to date in relation to the products. However, the recall is linked to a recent salmonella outbreak, which led to a recall of jalapeños that were distributed nationwide by Coast Citrus Distributors, a San Diego-based company with suppliers in the U.S. and Mexico. The affected jalapeños, supplied by a grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, were distributed in 26 states and have been connected to hundreds of cases of illness.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the outbreak has sickened at least 431 people, including 86 recent cases. Fifty-seven people have been hospitalized across 32 states.

The CDC explains that if you have the potentially contaminated jalapeños or products made from them, you should immediately throw them out.

The organization also listed a host of symptoms that could result from eating something contaminated with salmonella. These include diarrhea and a fever higher than 102 degrees, diarrhea for more than two days that is not improving, bloody diarrhea, so much vomiting that you cannot keep liquids down, and signs of dehydration such as not urinating enough, feeling dizzy, and a dry throat and mouth.

The CDC says that while most people recover in about four to seven days, adults older than 65, children younger than 5, and those with weakened immune systems are at a heightened risk for “more severe illnesses” due to salmonella.

A Whole Foods spokesperson told People magazine in an email: “Nothing matters more to us than our customers’ safety. We’ve pulled all recalled products from our shelves. Customers who purchased any of these products from us should throw them away and contact us for a refund.”

title: My Experience Has Nuance, Yours Is a Data Point
description:
Eric Bailey has a fun little post about how we need more than a few icons to express the nuance of our shared human experience.

For example, he suggests Netflix provide some feedback buttons to indicate the kinds of experiences we all share consuming and rating media:

  • “Just because I expressed interest in this show does not mean I want to be inundated with recommendations for its genre”
  • “Disregard [that I pressed ‘thumbs up’] my cat walked over the keyboard”
  • “I am making bad choices and hatewatching this” (which reminds me of )

What’s great about the examples in Eric’s post is how familiar they are. We can read them and laugh because we’ve had the same thought — “I’m pressing ‘thumbs up’ here, but what I really mean is…”

We know when we click that button that it’s a reductive expression of our experience that’ll be erroneously interpreted, but we do it anyway. As Bryan Cantrill shared from his experience:

There's no way to indicate, “I’m engaging with this, but I hate myself for doing it.” I need another mouse button that is like, “I’m clicking on this, but I’m rage clicking on it and for my own mental health could you not drag more of this in front of me please?”

We know these feedback mechanisms are often a misrepresentation of our actual experience.

Yet we turn around in our professional contexts and see numbers like “142,432 users gave this a ‘thumbs up’” and we forget everything we knew about our own individual experience with these systems. We make it mean what we want it to mean, what’s convenient for measurement and reporting e.g. “Wow, what a great insight about our offerings! Let’s restructure our entire catalog around this new, objective, (pseudo)scientific fact that so many people obviously like this thing!”

We reduce the experiences of others to mere data, but grant ourselves exemption from such oversimplifications.

Where’s the conversation around:

  • Values, e.g. “Should we provide more of this? We can say no to the data…”
  • Nuance, e.g. “What do people really mean when they click ‘thumbs up’ in this interface?”
  • Vision, e.g. “If we provide more of this, where will that lead us?”

But that’s too introspective. Introspection is slow. Ain’t nobody got time for that.

title: Laser tech detects fake alcohol bottles non-invasively
description:
Methanol poisoning from contaminated alcohol is relatively rare in countries with strict alcohol regulation, but it remains a serious problem in regions where counterfeit alcohol is common. Outbreaks continue to occur every year, causing deaths, blindness, and permanent injuries. A few years ago in Laos, six foreign tourists died after drinking at a backpacker hostel, and an even bigger outbreak occurred in Turkey in 2025, taking the lives of 160 people and leaving more than 250 incapacitated. Both cases were attributed to methanol poisoning from illegally produced alcohol.

title: Nissan and Honda partner to develop software for cars
description:
Japanese automakers Nissan and Honda entered a deal to jointly develop computer parts and software for vehicles set to enter the market in fiscal 2029, both sides said Monday.

Under the deal, Nissan, based in the port city of Yokohama, and Tokyo-based Honda will share standardized parts in “core ECUs,” or electronic control units, as well as software.

Nissan and Honda started talks in 2024 to work together in developing electric vehicles and auto intelligence technology.

Nissan makes Leaf electric cars and Infiniti luxury models, while Honda makes the Accord sedan, Civic compact, and Odyssey minivan.

Monday’s agreement did not specifically mention EVs, or any model names, and was focused on so-called software-defined vehicles, which could include EVs. These vehicles have functions and features that can be updated and controlled by software, rather than the mechanics of hardware.

The global competition in the auto industry is increasingly intensifying as it moves into various technologies, such as automated driving and zero emissions. Each vehicle is starting to be more like a computer packed with electronic parts and software rather than the old image of gas-guzzling engines.

Sharing components and collaborating on research will help cut costs and speed up development, as well as add efficiency in economies of scale once the vehicles go into production.

European makers Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Stellantis are working together in software development so they can share the same operating system.

Both Nissan and Honda are overshadowed by Toyota Motor Corp., the top Japanese automaker, and working together could be a plus in competing against Toyota.

However, Toyota has been mentioned in the past as engaging in the software talks with Nissan and Honda, although it was not part of Monday’s announcement.

Toyota is working on software with other companies like Subaru, which is part of the Toyota group, and U.S. autonomous driving technology company Waymo.

As part of their strategic partnership, Nissan and Honda will continue to explore other opportunities for collaboration across a range of areas, including zero-emissions and decreasing traffic fatalities.

Both sides stressed that the use of intelligence and electrification technology is an important focus for working together.

“Recognizing the need to strengthen competitiveness through faster development cycles and more efficient investment, the two companies have conducted extensive studies on potential collaboration in the software domain,” they said in a statement.

—By Yuri Kageyama, AP business writer

title: Rouxinol House / Sergio Sampaio Archi + Tectônica
description:
Concept
The 2,000-square-meter site of Rouxinol House, located in the Paraíba Valley in São Paulo, presented significant challenges in defining the architectural design. While it offered magnificent views of the Jaguari River reservoir, the design also had to address a 50-meter slope and the presence of over 300 surveyed trees. Minimizing environmental impact was non-negotiable—a combination of factors that determined the design decisions from the initial concept to the specification of materials.

title: Flash flood in Grand Canyon leaves 1 dead and several missing, National Park Service says
description:
One person died and about 15 people are missing or unaccounted for after a major flash flood at the Grand Canyon forced evacuations, pushed large boulders into the Colorado River and knocked out the sole water pipeline that serves tourists and residents, the National Park Service said Sunday.

The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said without providing additional details. Officials from an Arizona coroner’s office were on scene.

The flooding Saturday in Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the river, led to more than 60 people being airlifted from the depths of the canyon. The park service asked anyone with details about hikers or campers still unaccounted for to get in touch. The Arizona Department of Public Safety was helping with additional evacuations Sunday.

The limited potable water supply because of the damaged pipeline means tourists won’t be able to stay overnight at lodges and hotels within the park, starting Monday. Year-round residents are being asked to conserve water.

“These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park said in a statement.

Visiting the Grand Canyon — a crown jewel of the national park system — can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon, or rainy season. Clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.

Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with fellow physicians and a park ranger when heavy rain started falling Saturday.
“We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” he said.

Later, as they made their way toward Phantom Ranch, a colleague shouted “Up, Up, Up, Up!” as a 4-foot (1-meter) debris wall headed toward them and they ran up into a patch of cacti, he said. They were rescued by helicopter late Saturday after making it to the Phantom Ranch area, he said.

Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and extending an existing river rapid or creating a new one. The flood was a major blow to an enduring effort to modernize the pipeline that serves 6 million visitors a year and roughly 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.

“Heaven help us if the whole thing down there at the bottom has to be reconstructed,” said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University. “Where are they going to get the money?”

Halting overnight stays at the park because of a lack of water is rare, although the pipeline frequently has failed over the years. While the Grand Canyon has large storage tanks for potable water on the South Rim, they won’t be refilled while the pipeline is out of service.

A $208 million rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year.

Popular tourist spots, including the Bright Angel Campground, the North Kaibab Trail and Phantom Ranch, home to a historic canteen and dormitories, remained closed Sunday. Lodging is still available just outside the park’s South Rim entrance station in Tusayan.

Erica Viola said she and about 50 other hikers at that campground watched the creek rise Saturday and debris start to flow by, including what looked like a bunkhouse. The helicopter ride out cut her adventure short by two days, she said.

About half an inch to 1 inch (1 to 2.5 cm) of rain fell within about 20 minutes on a rocky slope where there’s a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Darren McCollum in Flagstaff. The deluge was preceded by two smaller systems that drenched the area hours earlier.

“So when the main storm moved in, torrential rain fell on everything that was already soaked, and that caused all the problems that we’re seeing,” McCollum said.

The weather service said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, dropping around 6,000 feet (1,828 meters).

More rain and thunderstorms were possible for the area into Monday.

Jeffrey Collins, Holly Ramer, and Christopher Weber also contributed.

—Jamie Stengle and Felicia Fonseca, Associated Press
